title: Command and Scripting Interpreter: AppleScript
summary: AppleScript is a macOS scripting language that controls applications and parts of the operating system through inter-application messages called Apple events. Those events can locate open windows, send keystrokes and interact with almost any running application, locally or across a remote session, without a new program being installed. Scripts run through the command line scripting utility, from a script file, or from host features such as mail rules, calendar alarms and automation workflows, and they can also be invoked from compiled binaries through the native scripting interfaces so that no command line tool appears at all. Because AppleScript reaches capabilities that would otherwise need a compiled binary, adversaries use it to present fake credential dialogs, drive an already open remote connection, move to other machines and launch further payloads. Detection combines process creation for the scripting utility and its parent, script text visible in process arguments, Apple event activity between application pairs that normally do not talk, and script files that are unsigned or stored in unusual locations. Legitimate automation generates the same events, so a documented baseline is essential.

beginner.definition: AppleScript is a scripting language built into macOS computers. A script is a short set of instructions that a computer follows, rather like a recipe. AppleScript can tell other applications what to do, for example opening a window, reading text or typing keys. Attackers use it because it can control programs already on the machine without installing anything new.
beginner.whyItMatters: AppleScript is already part of the system, so nothing suspicious needs to be installed first. It can control applications that are already open, including a remote session or a mail program. Scripts can also be triggered by everyday features such as mail rules, which many people never think about. The activity often looks exactly like normal automation. That is why defenders treat script contents and parents as evidence, not only files.
howItWorks: A script is a list of instructions written in a language the computer can run.
AppleScript controls other applications by sending them messages, which are called Apple events.
A script can start from a terminal, a file, a mail rule or a calendar alarm.
The script can read open windows, press keys and move data between programs.
It can also start other tools, so a small script becomes the first step of a chain.
Compiled programs can run AppleScript directly, so no scripting command appears in the process list.
beginner.example: Think of a large hotel with a staff intercom system. Any employee can pick up the handset and ask another department for help. Someone might ask for a door to be opened. The intercom is part of the building and needs no special tool. A visitor who learns the right phrases can make staff act. The intercom log looks the same as any normal request. Nobody installed anything, and the work still gets done.
takeaways: AppleScript is a built in macOS tool that controls applications by sending messages.
It can be triggered by normal features such as mail rules, not only by a person.
Script contents and parent processes matter more than a single file name.

objectives: Explain what AppleScript and Apple events are in simple terms.
Describe several ways an AppleScript can be started on a macOS host.
Explain how a script can control applications without starting a new program.
Identify process and script evidence that reveals AppleScript abuse.
Explain why normal administrative automation makes allow listing important.
